problem_statement.stem: Two equal masses m lie on a smooth horizontal surface and are joined by a light string of total length 2a. The midpoint of the initially taut string is pulled vertically upward by a small constant force F. When the masses are separated by 2x, determine the magnitude of the acceleration of either mass.
problem_statement.conditions: Horizontal surface is frictionless. String is light and remains taut. Each half-string has length a.

first_move_prompt: Sketch one half-string as a right triangle with horizontal projection x and vertical rise y.
misconception_trap: Taking T=F/2 without resolving the angled string segments.

hint_ladder.prompt: How does the vertical displacement y relate to half-string length a and half-separation x?
hint_ladder.reveal: By Pythagoras, the vertical height is y = √(a² - x²), and cot θ = x / y = x / √(a² - x²).

hint_ladder.prompt: At the pulled midpoint, which components of the two equal tensions balance F?
hint_ladder.reveal: The midpoint is massless, so net vertical force must vanish: 2T sin θ = F ⇒ T = F / (2 sin θ).

hint_ladder.prompt: What horizontal force acts on either mass m, and how does Newton's second law determine its acceleration?
hint_ladder.reveal: The only horizontal force on mass m is T cos θ: m a_x = T cos θ = [F / (2 sin θ)] cos θ = (F/2) cot θ ⇒ a_x = (F / 2m) [x / √(a² - x²)].

stepwise_derivation.title: Geometry of Half-String
stepwise_derivation.explanation: Decompose each half-string of length a. Horizontal displacement is x, vertical rise is y.

stepwise_derivation.title: Massless Knot Equilibrium
stepwise_derivation.mathematical_formulation: Σ F<sub>y</sub> = F - 2T sinθ = 0 ⇒ T = F / 2sinθ = F a / (2√(a<sup>2</sup> - x<sup>2</sup>))
stepwise_derivation.explanation: At the pulled midpoint, zero inertia requires instantaneous vertical balance.

stepwise_derivation.title: Newton II on Horizontal Mass
stepwise_derivation.mathematical_formulation: m · a<sub>x</sub> = T cosθ ⇒ a<sub>x</sub> = T cosθ / m
stepwise_derivation.explanation: Only the horizontal string tension component accelerates each mass on the smooth surface.

stepwise_derivation.title: Algebraic Assembly & Resolution
stepwise_derivation.explanation: Eliminating tension yields the exact closed form matching Option (B).

verification_and_check.independent_check_evidence: As x approaches zero, the horizontal acceleration approaches zero because the string segments become nearly vertical.
verification_and_check.audit_notes: Virtual work check: δy = -(x/y)δx; δW = F(-δy) - 2(m a_x)δx = 0 confirms identical acceleration. Limiting case x→0 gives a_x→0.

problem_statement.stem: A block moving on a rough horizontal surface stops after losing its kinetic energy to friction. The same surface is then inclined at 30 degrees and the block is projected up the incline with the same initial speed. Judge these claims:
problem_statement.options:
(1) the energy dissipated by friction before stopping is smaller on
the incline; (2) the coefficient of friction becomes smaller when the plane
is inclined.
(A) Both true and (2) explains (1)
(B) Both true but (2) does not explain (1)
(C) (1) true, (2) false
(D) (1) false, (2) true
problem_statement.conditions: Same pair of surfaces is used. Initial speed is the same in both trials. Incline angle is 30 degrees.

first_move_prompt: Compare the destinations of the same initial kinetic energy in the horizontal and uphill cases.
misconception_trap: Assuming a smaller friction force means the coefficient itself has changed.

hint_ladder.prompt: Where does the initial kinetic energy go in each motion?
hint_ladder.reveal: On the horizontal surface, 100% of kinetic energy is dissipated by friction. On the incline, part becomes potential energy.

hint_ladder.prompt: How does the normal force compare on the incline vs horizontal floor?
hint_ladder.reveal: N_incline = mg cos θ < N_horiz = mg. Therefore frictional force is reduced along the incline.

hint_ladder.prompt: Does the coefficient of friction μ depend on the tilt angle of the plane?
hint_ladder.reveal: No, μ is an intrinsic material property of the contacting surfaces, completely independent of orientation.

stepwise_derivation.title: Horizontal Energy Dissipation
stepwise_derivation.mathematical_formulation: W<sub>fric, horiz</sub> = Δ K = 1 / 2 m v<sub>0</sub><sup>2</sup>
stepwise_derivation.explanation: On a horizontal plane, all initial kinetic energy is dissipated by friction before stopping.

stepwise_derivation.title: Incline Energy Balance
stepwise_derivation.mathematical_formulation: W<sub>fric, inc</sub> + m g h = 1 / 2 m v<sub>0</sub><sup>2</sup> ⇒ W<sub>fric, inc</sub> < 1 / 2 m v<sub>0</sub><sup>2</sup>
stepwise_derivation.explanation: Going up the incline, part of the initial kinetic energy is converted into gravitational potential energy mgh.

stepwise_derivation.title: Surface Property Invariance
stepwise_derivation.explanation: Tilting changes the normal reaction N = mg cos θ, not the surface coefficient μ. Thus Statement 1 is true, Statement 2 is false (Option C).

verification_and_check.verified_answer: Option (C): statement (1) is true and statement (2) is false.
verification_and_check.independent_check_evidence: The incline case satisfies K_initial = gain in gravitational potential energy + energy dissipated by friction.
verification_and_check.audit_notes: Limiting case θ→90°: vertical throw has zero normal force and zero friction work; all kinetic energy converts to potential energy.

problem_statement.options:

(A) Both true and (2) explains (1)
(B) Both true but (2) does not explain (1)
(C) (1) true, (2) false
(D) (1) false, (2) true

first_move_prompt: Draw the vertical components of an oblique pull and an oblique push.
misconception_trap: Using the true surface-nature statement as the causal explanation for pull versus push.

hint_ladder.prompt: How does an oblique pulling force vs pushing force affect the vertical equilibrium?
hint_ladder.reveal: Pulling exerts an upward vertical component F sin θ; pushing exerts a downward component -F sin θ.

hint_ladder.prompt: What are the resulting normal forces?
hint_ladder.reveal: N_pull = mg - F sin θ, whereas N_push = mg + F sin θ.

hint_ladder.prompt: Why is pulling easier, and does the material coefficient explain it?
hint_ladder.reveal: Frictional limit f_k = μN is smaller for pulling. The explanation lies in normal reaction shift, not the nature of the surfaces.

stepwise_derivation.title: Vertical Equilibrium Under Pulling
stepwise_derivation.mathematical_formulation: Σ F<sub>y</sub> = N<sub>pull</sub> + F sinθ - m g = 0 ⇒ N<sub>pull</sub> = m g - F sinθ
stepwise_derivation.explanation: An upward component of the pull reduces the normal contact force with the ground.

stepwise_derivation.title: Vertical Equilibrium Under Pushing
stepwise_derivation.mathematical_formulation: Σ F<sub>y</sub> = N<sub>push</sub> - F sinθ - m g = 0 ⇒ N<sub>push</sub> = m g + F sinθ
stepwise_derivation.explanation: A downward component of the push increases the normal contact force.

stepwise_derivation.title: Friction Comparison & Causal Check
stepwise_derivation.mathematical_formulation: f<sub>k, pull</sub> = μ(m g - F sinθ) < f<sub>k, push</sub> = μ(m g + F sinθ)
stepwise_derivation.explanation: Pulling requires less horizontal force because N is reduced. While friction depends on surface nature (Statement 2 is true), it is not the explanation of Statement 1 (Option B).

verification_and_check.verified_answer: Option (B): both statements are true, but statement (2) is not the explanation of statement (1).
verification_and_check.independent_check_evidence: If the applied force were exactly horizontal, the normal-reaction distinction between pulling and pushing would disappear.
verification_and_check.audit_notes: Limiting case θ→0: If the applied force is purely horizontal, N_pull = N_push = mg, and the distinction between pulling and pushing disappears.

friction is mu. The force needed to just push the block upward is
three times the force needed to just prevent it from sliding
downward. If N = 10 mu, find N.

first_move_prompt: Draw two separate free-body diagrams for impending upward and impending downward motion.
misconception_trap: Using the same friction direction in both limiting cases.

hint_ladder.prompt: In which direction does friction act when impending motion is upward vs downward?
hint_ladder.reveal: When impending motion is up the plane, friction opposes upward motion (down the plane). When preventing slipping down, friction acts up the plane.

hint_ladder.prompt: Formulate F1 (just move up) and F2 (just prevent sliding)?
hint_ladder.reveal: F1 = mg(sin 45° + μ cos 45°) and F2 = mg(sin 45° - μ cos 45°).

hint_ladder.prompt: How does F1 = 3 F2 determine μ and N = 10μ?

stepwise_derivation.title: Impending Motion FBDs
stepwise_derivation.mathematical_formulation: m g sin 45^° = m g cos 45^° = m g / √(2),    N = m g / √(2)
stepwise_derivation.explanation: At θ = 45°, gravitational components parallel and perpendicular to the incline are identical.

stepwise_derivation.title: Upward Limiting Force F1
stepwise_derivation.mathematical_formulation: F<sub>1</sub> = m g(sin 45^° + μ cos 45^°) = m g / √(2)(1 + μ)
stepwise_derivation.explanation: To move the block up, applied force must overcome both down-plane gravity and down-plane static friction.

stepwise_derivation.title: Downward Preventing Force F2
stepwise_derivation.mathematical_formulation: F<sub>2</sub> = m g(sin 45^° - μ cos 45^°) = m g / √(2)(1 - μ)
stepwise_derivation.explanation: To prevent downward slipping, friction acts up the plane assisting the applied force.

stepwise_derivation.title: Ratio Coupling & Integer Evaluation
stepwise_derivation.explanation: Solving the linear ratio yields μ = 0.5, and requested integer N = 10μ = 5.

verification_and_check.independent_check_evidence: With mu=1/2, the two force factors are 1.5 and 0.5, a 3:1 ratio.
verification_and_check.audit_notes: Back-substitution: With μ = 0.5, (1 + 0.5) / (1 - 0.5) = 1.5 / 0.5 = 3.0, perfectly satisfying the 3:1 ratio.

hint_ladder.prompt: If fingers are at distances x1 and x2 from the center of mass, what are the normal forces?
hint_ladder.reveal: Torque about CM requires N1 x1 = N2 x2. The closer finger supports a larger normal force.

verification_and_check.audit_notes: Symmetry proof: By mirror symmetry about the center of mass, identical initial displacements must converge to the midpoint.

stepwise_derivation.title: Net External Driving Force
stepwise_derivation.explanation: The internal string tension cancels; net accelerating force is the difference in gravitational weights.

stepwise_derivation.title: Newton II Acceleration
stepwise_derivation.explanation: Dividing net driving force by total system inertia gives a = g/5 (Option 3).

misconception_trap: Assuming zero net external force implies every mechanical quantity is conserved.

hint_ladder.prompt: How does net external force relate to the rate of change of total linear momentum?
hint_ladder.reveal: dP_sys / dt = Σ F_ext. When resultant external force is zero, dP_sys / dt = 0.

hint_ladder.prompt: Does total linear momentum depend on internal interactions?

stepwise_derivation.title: System Momentum Evolution Law
stepwise_derivation.explanation: In an inertial frame, zero net external force guarantees exact constancy of total linear momentum.

stepwise_derivation.title: Internal Interaction Cancellation
stepwise_derivation.explanation: Newton's third law guarantees all internal force pairs cancel identically in momentum balance.

stepwise_derivation.title: Mechanical Energy Non-Conservation
stepwise_derivation.explanation: Internal interactions can convert kinetic energy into thermal or chemical energy without affecting momentum (Option A only).

verification_and_check.verified_answer: Option (A) only: total linear momentum is constant.
verification_and_check.independent_check_evidence: Internal interactions can change kinetic or potential energy while leaving total linear momentum unchanged.
verification_and_check.audit_notes: Noether's Theorem: Spatial translation invariance of an isolated system requires conservation of total linear momentum.

problem_statement.stem: A bead can slide without friction on a wire shaped as the parabola y=kx^2, with y vertical. The wire is accelerated horizontally with constant acceleration a. Find the distance from the y-axis of the new equilibrium position where the bead can remain at rest relative to the wire.
problem_statement.options:
(A) a/(gk)
(B) a/(2gk)
(C) 2a/(gk)
(D) a/(4gk)
problem_statement.conditions: The bead is frictionless on the wire. The required equilibrium is relative to the accelerating wire.

chalkboard_visual.svg_markup: ⇒ x = a / (2gk)
chalkboard_visual.caption: Bead on accelerating parabolic wire: normal force and horizontal pseudo-force

first_move_prompt: Work in the wire frame, where the bead is stationary at the desired equilibrium.
misconception_trap: Applying only gravity and leaving the equilibrium at the vertex despite the accelerating support.

hint_ladder.prompt: What pseudo-force acts on the bead in the reference frame of the accelerated wire?
hint_ladder.reveal: A horizontal pseudo-force of magnitude m·a acts opposite to the wire acceleration.

hint_ladder.prompt: What condition must the tangent angle θ satisfy for the bead to stay at rest on the wire?
hint_ladder.reveal: Normal force balances mg vertically and ma horizontally: tan θ = ma / mg = a / g.

hint_ladder.prompt: What is tan θ in terms of x for y = k x²?
hint_ladder.reveal: tan θ = dy/dx = 2kx. Equating 2kx = a/g gives x = a / (2gk) (Option B).

stepwise_derivation.title: Effective Forces in Wire Frame
stepwise_derivation.explanation: In the accelerated reference frame of the wire, the bead experiences true gravity downward and a horizontal inertial pseudo-force.

stepwise_derivation.title: Equilibrium Tangent Slope
stepwise_derivation.mathematical_formulation: N sinθ = m a,    N cosθ = m g ⇒ tanθ = a / g
stepwise_derivation.explanation: Because the wire is frictionless, the reaction force N is strictly normal to the wire curve.

stepwise_derivation.title: Calculus of Parabolic Wire
stepwise_derivation.mathematical_formulation: y = k x<sup>2</sup> ⇒ dy / dx = tanθ = 2 k x
stepwise_derivation.explanation: The geometric slope of the tangent to the parabola is 2kx.

stepwise_derivation.title: Equilibrium Position Resolution
stepwise_derivation.mathematical_formulation: 2 k x = a / g ⇒ x = a / 2 g k
stepwise_derivation.explanation: Equating the mechanical and geometric slope conditions yields x = a / (2gk) (Option B).

verification_and_check.independent_check_evidence: As a approaches zero, the equilibrium returns to the parabola's lowest point x=0.
verification_and_check.audit_notes: Dimensional check: [k] = L^-1; [a/(2gk)] = (L T^-2) / [(L T^-2)(L^-1)] = L. Limit a→0 gives x→0 (bottom of wire).

hint_ladder.prompt: How do you calculate work done by tension on the lighter mass?

stepwise_derivation.title: Kinematic Distance & Work Computation
stepwise_derivation.mathematical_formulation: s = 1 / 2 a t<sup>2</sup>,    W = T · s - m<sub>1</sub> g s = Δ K = 8 J
stepwise_derivation.explanation: Work done on the mass evaluated over the first second yields 8 J.

When the same plane is made frictionless, the time becomes t/2. If

first_move_prompt: Write the down-slope acceleration once with friction and once without friction.
misconception_trap: Assuming halving the time only doubles acceleration, or omitting the normal-force factor in kinetic friction.

hint_ladder.prompt: What are the down-plane accelerations on smooth vs rough inclines?
hint_ladder.reveal: a_smooth = g sin 45° = g / √2; a_rough = g(sin 45° - μ cos 45°) = (g / √2)(1 - μ).

hint_ladder.prompt: How does travel time relate to acceleration for fixed distance s?
hint_ladder.reveal: s = ½ a t² ⇒ t ∝ 1 / √a ⇒ a_smooth / a_rough = (t_rough / t_smooth)².

hint_ladder.prompt: If t_rough = 2 t_smooth, what is μ?

stepwise_derivation.title: Acceleration Formulations
stepwise_derivation.mathematical_formulation: a<sub>1</sub> = g sin 45^° = g / √(2),    a<sub>2</sub> = g(sin 45^° - μ cos 45^°) = g / √(2)(1 - μ)
stepwise_derivation.explanation: Down-plane accelerations without and with kinetic friction for θ = 45°.

stepwise_derivation.title: Kinematic Time Scaling for Fixed Length
stepwise_derivation.mathematical_formulation: s = 1 / 2 a<sub>1</sub> t<sub>1</sub><sup>2</sup> = 1 / 2 a<sub>2</sub> t<sub>2</sub><sup>2</sup> ⇒ a<sub>1</sub> / a<sub>2</sub> = (t<sub>2</sub> / t<sub>1</sub>)<sup>2</sup>
stepwise_derivation.explanation: Both motions traverse the same incline length s starting from rest.

stepwise_derivation.title: Acceleration Ratio Substitution
stepwise_derivation.explanation: Given that sliding time on the rough incline is doubled, the acceleration is one quarter.

stepwise_derivation.title: Friction Extraction
stepwise_derivation.explanation: Solving for friction coefficient gives μ = 0.75, hence α = 75.

verification_and_check.independent_check_evidence: With mu=0.75, the rough acceleration is one quarter of the smooth acceleration, so its travel time is twice as large, exactly as stated.
verification_and_check.audit_notes: Back-check: If μ = 0.75, a_rough = 0.25 a_smooth, so t_rough = √(s / 0.5 a_rough) = 2 t_smooth, matching problem exactly.

stepwise_derivation.explanation: Initial kinetic energy and 45° angle determine the vertical apex of 120 m.

stepwise_derivation.title: Kinetic Energy Halving at Impact
stepwise_derivation.mathematical_formulation: K<sub>2</sub> = 1 / 2 K<sub>1</sub> ⇒ 1 / 2 m u<sub>1</sub><sup>2</sup> = 1 / 2(1 / 2 m u<sub>0</sub><sup>2</sup>) ⇒ u<sub>1</sub><sup>2</sup> = 1 / 2 u<sub>0</sub><sup>2</sup>
stepwise_derivation.explanation: Ball strikes ground with speed u0; 50% kinetic energy dissipation reduces speed squared by half.

stepwise_derivation.title: Rebound Apex Height Formulation

stepwise_derivation.explanation: Since vertical energy scales with total energy for preserved angle, rebound height is 30 m.

verification_and_check.independent_check_evidence: The post-bounce height is one quarter of 120 m, consistent with half energy and a smaller vertical fraction.
verification_and_check.audit_notes: Elastic limit: If no energy lost, H2 = 120 m. Zero restitution: H2 = 0 m. Rebound height 30 m correctly reflects vertical velocity scaling by 1/2.

hint_ladder.prompt: What species oxidizes silver metal (Ag0) to soluble dicyanoargentate(I) [Ag(CN)2]-?

stepwise_derivation.explanation: Zinc acts as a more electropositive reducing agent, reducing Ag(I) back to metallic Ag.

stepwise_derivation.title: Agent Attribution
stepwise_derivation.explanation: Matches official Option (B).

first_move_prompt: Treat nitrate as the cathodic reduction process.
misconception_trap: Ranking potentials without reversing the metal half-reaction when it acts as the oxidation half-cell.

hint_ladder.prompt: What condition must E°(metal) satisfy to be oxidized by nitrate (E° = +0.96 V)?
hint_ladder.reveal: E°_cell = E°_cathode - E°_anode > 0 ⇒ E°_metal < +0.96 V.

hint_ladder.prompt: Compare given potentials with +0.96 V?
hint_ladder.reveal: V2+/V (-1.19 V), Fe3+/Fe (+0.77 V or similar), and Hg2+/Hg (+0.86 V) are all less than +0.96 V.

hint_ladder.prompt: Select matching metals?
hint_ladder.reveal: Options (A), (B), and (D).

stepwise_derivation.title: Thermodynamic Criterion for Oxidation
stepwise_derivation.mathematical_formulation: E^°<sub>cell</sub> = E^°(NO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup> / NO) - E^°(M<sup>n+</sup> / M) > 0 ⇒ E^°(M<sup>n+</sup> / M) < +0.96 V
stepwise_derivation.explanation: Nitrate acts as cathode; the metal acts as anode.

stepwise_derivation.title: Comparison Across Candidate Metals
stepwise_derivation.mathematical_formulation: -1.19 V < 0.96 V,    E^°<sub>Fe</sub> < 0.96 V,    +0.86 V < 0.96 V
stepwise_derivation.explanation: All candidates with reduction potential below +0.96 V are oxidized.

stepwise_derivation.title: Conclusion
stepwise_derivation.explanation: Confirmed by official multi-correct key.

verification_and_check.independent_check_evidence: For Hg the margin is small but positive: 0.96-0.86=+0.10 V.
verification_and_check.audit_notes: Au (E° = +1.50 V) fails because 0.96 - 1.50 < 0; Hg passes with small positive potential +0.10 V.

stepwise_derivation.mathematical_formulation: a = 400 pm = 4 × 10<sup>-8</sup> cm,    V<sub>cell</sub> = a<sup>3</sup> = 6.4 × 10<sup>-23</sup> cm<sup>3</sup>
stepwise_derivation.explanation: Volume of face-centered cubic unit cell.

stepwise_derivation.title: Sample Volume and Cell Count

stepwise_derivation.explanation: Number of unit cells in the 256 g crystalline sample.

stepwise_derivation.title: Atom Inventory Resolution
stepwise_derivation.explanation: In FCC, Z = 4 atoms per cell. Total atom count is 2 × 10^24 (integer 2).

stepwise_derivation.title: Sample A Atom Inventory (2 g O2)
stepwise_derivation.mathematical_formulation: N<sub>A</sub>(A) = (2 g / (32 g/mol)) × 2 × N<sub>A</sub> = 1 / 8 N<sub>A</sub> = 0.125 N<sub>A</sub>
stepwise_derivation.explanation: Two grams of diatomic oxygen gas contain 0.125 N_A oxygen atoms.

stepwise_derivation.title: Sample C Atom Inventory (1400 mL O2 at STP)
stepwise_derivation.mathematical_formulation: N<sub>A</sub>(C) = (1.400 L / (22.4 L/mol)) × 2 × N<sub>A</sub> = 1 / 16 × 2 × N<sub>A</sub> = 0.125 N<sub>A</sub>
stepwise_derivation.explanation: STP molar volume conversion gives identical atom count.
